name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q01 - Boron covalence, aluminium passivation, oxides, and borax

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four statements regarding Group 13 elements and their compounds:

Statement I: Boron cannot form the \(\left[\mathrm{BF}_6\right]^{3-}\) ion because of the non-availability of \(d\)-orbitals in its valence shell, which limits its maximum covalence to \(4\).

Statement II: Concentrated nitric acid renders aluminium passive by forming a protective oxide layer on the metal surface.

Statement III: Boron trioxide (\(\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)) is basic in nature, whereas thallium(III) oxide (\(\mathrm{Tl}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)) is strongly acidic.

Statement IV: On strong heating, borax swells up and solidifies into a transparent glass-like bead composed of sodium metaborate and boric anhydride.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle — Maximum Covalence of Boron
Boron is a second-period element with electronic configuration \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^1\). Because its valence shell (\(n = 2\)) contains only one \(2s\) orbital and three \(2p\) orbitals and lacks \(d\)-orbitals, boron can accommodate a maximum of four electron pairs and cannot expand its octet beyond a covalence of \(4\). Therefore, while \(\left[\mathrm{BF}_4\right]^-\) exists, \(\left[\mathrm{BF}_6\right]^{3-}\) cannot be formed. Hence, the proposition regarding the inability of boron to form \(\left[\mathrm{BF}_6\right]^{3-}\) is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation — Passivation of Aluminium
Although aluminium dissolves in dilute hydrochloric acid and aqueous alkalies, concentrated nitric acid oxidises the surface of aluminium to form a very thin, impervious protective layer of aluminium oxide (\(\mathrm{Al}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)) that prevents further reaction. Thus, aluminium becomes passive in concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\). Hence, the proposition regarding the passivation of aluminium is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation — Acidic and Basic Character of Group 13 Oxides
Down Group 13, metallic character increases, so the nature of the oxides changes from acidic to amphoteric to basic. Boron trioxide (\(\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)) is acidic and reacts with basic metallic oxides to form metal borates, aluminium and gallium oxides are amphoteric, and indium and thallium oxides (\(\mathrm{Tl}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)) are basic. Reversing their acidic and basic character makes that proposition incorrect.

Step 4: Application — Thermal Decomposition of Borax
When borax (\(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{B}_4\mathrm{O}_7\cdot 10\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)) is heated, it first loses water molecules and swells up. On further heating, it melts into a transparent liquid that solidifies into a glass-like material (borax bead) consisting of sodium metaborate (\(\mathrm{NaBO}_2\)) and boric anhydride (\(\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)). Hence, the proposition regarding the borax bead composition is correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The propositions concerning the maximum covalence of boron, the passivation of aluminium in concentrated nitric acid, and the formation of a glass-like bead of sodium metaborate and boric anhydride from borax are correct, whereas the proposition reversing the acid-base nature of boron and thallium oxides is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q02 - Catenation, carbon allotropes, and carbon monoxide toxicity

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the following four statements regarding carbon, its allotropes, and carbon monoxide:

Statement I: The tendency for catenation among Group 14 elements decreases in the order \(\mathrm{C} \gg \mathrm{Si} > \mathrm{Ge} \approx \mathrm{Sn}\), while lead does not show catenation.

Statement II: In Buckminsterfullerene (\(\mathrm{C}_{60}\)), each carbon atom is \(sp^3\) hybridised and forms four \(\sigma\)-bonds with neighbouring carbon atoms.

Statement III: Carbon monoxide is highly poisonous because it forms a complex with haemoglobin that is about \(300\) times more stable than the oxygen-haemoglobin complex.

Statement IV: Graphite conducts electricity along its layers because each carbon atom is \(sp^2\) hybridised and its fourth valence electron is delocalised over the hexagonal sheet.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle — Catenation in Group 14
Catenation is the ability of atoms of an element to link with one another through covalent bonds to form chains and rings. Because \(\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{C}\) bonds have a very high bond enthalpy (\(348\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)), carbon exhibits strong catenation. Down Group 14, atomic size increases, electronegativity decreases, and \(\mathrm{M}-\mathrm{M}\) bond enthalpy decreases (\(\mathrm{Si}-\mathrm{Si}: 297\), \(\mathrm{Ge}-\mathrm{Ge}: 260\), \(\mathrm{Sn}-\mathrm{Sn}: 240\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)), so catenation decreases as \(\mathrm{C} \gg \mathrm{Si} > \mathrm{Ge} \approx \mathrm{Sn}\), and lead does not show catenation. Hence, the proposition regarding the catenation trend in Group 14 is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation — Hybridisation in Buckminsterfullerene (\(\mathrm{C}_{60}\))
In \(\mathrm{C}_{60}\), all \(60\) carbon atoms are equivalent and undergo \(sp^2\) hybridisation, not \(sp^3\). Each carbon atom forms three \(\sigma\)-bonds with three neighbouring carbon atoms, while the fourth valence electron is delocalised in molecular orbitals, giving aromatic character to the cage-like molecule. Hence, the proposition describing \(\mathrm{C}_{60}\) as \(sp^3\) hybridised with four \(\sigma\)-bonds per carbon is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation — Poisonous Nature of Carbon Monoxide
Carbon monoxide (\(\mathrm{CO}\)) has a lone pair on the carbon atom and binds strongly to the iron of haemoglobin in red blood corpuscles. The resulting carboxyhaemoglobin complex is approximately \(300\) times more stable than the oxyhaemoglobin complex, preventing haemoglobin from transporting oxygen around the body and leading to death. Hence, the proposition explaining the toxicity of carbon monoxide is correct.

Step 4: Application — Electrical Conductivity of Graphite
Graphite consists of planar hexagonal layers in which each carbon atom is \(sp^2\) hybridised and forms three \(\sigma\)-bonds with three adjacent carbon atoms. The fourth valence electron forms a \(\pi\)-bond and is delocalised over the entire sheet. Because these delocalised electrons are mobile, graphite conducts electricity along the sheet. Hence, the proposition explaining electrical conduction in graphite is correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The propositions regarding the catenation order in Group 14, the stability of the \(\mathrm{CO}\)-haemoglobin complex, and the \(sp^2\) hybridisation with delocalised electrons in graphite are correct, whereas the proposition attributing \(sp^3\) hybridisation to Buckminsterfullerene is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q03 - Group 14 halides, silica reactivity, and zeolites

questiontext.text:
Examine the following four statements regarding Group 14 halides, silica, and zeolites:

Statement I: Among Group 14 tetrahalides (\(\mathrm{MX}_4\)), \(\mathrm{SnF}_4\) and \(\mathrm{PbF}_4\) are ionic in nature, whereas most other \(\mathrm{MX}_4\) halides are covalent and tetrahedral.

Statement II: Lead(IV) iodide (\(\mathrm{PbI}_4\)) does not exist because the \(\mathrm{Pb}-\mathrm{I}\) bond initially formed does not release enough energy to unpair the \(6s^2\) electrons and excite one of them to a higher orbital.

Statement III: Silicon dioxide (\(\mathrm{SiO}_2\)) is a three-dimensional covalent network solid that is completely unreactive towards both \(\mathrm{HF}\) and \(\mathrm{NaOH}\).

Statement IV: ZSM-5 is a type of zeolite used as a catalyst in the petrochemical industry to convert alcohols directly into gasoline.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle — Bonding in Group 14 Tetrahalides
Most Group 14 tetrahalides of formula \(\mathrm{MX}_4\) are covalent in nature with \(sp^3\) hybridisation of the central atom and a tetrahedral geometry. However, \(\mathrm{SnF}_4\) and \(\mathrm{PbF}_4\) are exceptions and are ionic in nature due to the high electronegativity of fluorine and the metallic character of tin and lead. Hence, the proposition regarding the ionic nature of \(\mathrm{SnF}_4\) and \(\mathrm{PbF}_4\) compared to other covalent tetrahedral \(\mathrm{MX}_4\) halides is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation — Non-Existence of \(\mathrm{PbI}_4\)
To form four covalent bonds around lead, the paired \(6s^2\) electrons must be unpaired and one electron excited to a \(6p\) orbital. The energy released during the formation of the weak \(\mathrm{Pb}-\mathrm{I}\) bond is not sufficient to supply this promotional energy, so \(\mathrm{PbI}_4\) does not exist. Hence, the proposition explaining why \(\mathrm{PbI}_4\) does not exist is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation — Chemical Reactivity of Silicon Dioxide (\(\mathrm{SiO}_2\))
Although \(\mathrm{SiO}_2\) is a three-dimensional covalent network solid with very high \(\mathrm{Si}-\mathrm{O}\) bond enthalpy and resists attack by halogens, dihydrogen, and most acids and metals, it is not completely unreactive. Specifically, \(\mathrm{SiO}_2\) reacts with \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) to form sodium silicate (\(\mathrm{SiO}_2 + 2\mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{SiO}_3 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)) and with \(\mathrm{HF}\) to form silicon tetrafluoride (\(\mathrm{SiO}_2 + 4\mathrm{HF} \rightarrow \mathrm{SiF}_4 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)). Hence, the proposition claiming that \(\mathrm{SiO}_2\) is completely unreactive towards \(\mathrm{HF}\) and \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) is incorrect.

Step 4: Application — Catalytic Use of ZSM-5 Zeolite
Zeolites are microporous aluminosilicates widely used as shape-selective catalysts in petrochemical industries for hydrocarbon cracking and isomerisation. In particular, the zeolite catalyst ZSM-5 is used to convert alcohols directly into gasoline. Hence, the proposition regarding the use of ZSM-5 is correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The propositions regarding the ionic character of \(\mathrm{SnF}_4\) and \(\mathrm{PbF}_4\), the non-existence of \(\mathrm{PbI}_4\), and the catalytic application of ZSM-5 are correct, whereas the proposition stating that \(\mathrm{SiO}_2\) is unreactive towards \(\mathrm{HF}\) and \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) is incorrect.
